title: Same word, different meaning
hook: early Christian writers used Stoic words like logos while believing something different (John 1:1)
carry: whose house is this word living in right now

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Fortune's wheel. Your line was the wheel turns, and Philosophy saying you always knew she turned.

Say the word football in London, then in Dallas. Same word, two different games, and a whole conversation can go sideways before anyone notices. Words travel, and when they move into a new house, they rearrange the furniture. One small Greek word made a move like that. The Stoics had used it long before. Then it turned up in the first line of a gospel. Today: logos.
screen: `FOOTBALL IN LONDON AND DALLAS.` → `WORDS MOVE HOUSE.` → `LOGOS.`

segments.voice: First, the Greek word. Logos means word, speech, account, reason, the reasoning behind a thing. Long before the Stoics, the philosopher Heraclitus used it for an order running through the world. For the Stoics, as in Cleanthes' hymn, the logos was the divine reason pervading everything, the world's own rational pattern, something like its soul. Second, the gospel. The Gospel of John opens, in the King James Version: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Word there is logos. A few lines later: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." For Christians, this Logos isn't an impersonal pattern spread through matter. It is a person, eternally with God, who became a human being, Jesus. Third, where it came from. Scholars debate how much John drew on Greek philosophy and how much on the Hebrew Bible, where God creates by speaking and sends out his word. Some readers hear both voices in the room. And a Jewish philosopher of the same era, Philo of Alexandria, also wrote at length about the Logos, in his own way. Fourth, the borrowing. Early Christian writers like Justin, the teacher from Marcus's reign, used the Stoic phrase seed-bearing logos to say that seeds of truth were scattered among the philosophers. Same word, different meanings: Stoics, Philo and the Christians each meant something of their own by it.
screen: `LOGOS: WORD, REASON, ACCOUNT.` · `JOHN 1:1: "IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD."` · `GREEK AND HEBREW VOICES IN THE ROOM.` · `JUSTIN BORROWS: SEEDS OF THE LOGOS.` · then, large: `SAME WORD, DIFFERENT MEANING.`

segments.voice: Think of a word that you and someone close to you use differently: love, faith, freedom, home. Say what it means to you in one sentence, then try, honestly, to say what it means to them in theirs. Just see the gap; some arguments live right there, between two meanings of one word.
Logos. Greek for word and reason. For Stoics, the reason running through the world; for John's gospel, the Word who was with God and became flesh. Today's word.
Your line: whose house is this word living in right now. A familiar word can still be a guest. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians read John 1 as the Logos, the Word of God, becoming human in Jesus; students of philosophy trace the same Greek word through Heraclitus, the Stoics and Philo, each with its own meaning.

chat.says: Is the logos in John's gospel the same as the Stoics' logos?
options: Same Greek word, but John means a person, the Word made flesh; Stoics, reason in all.
Yes, John simply took over the Stoic idea of a reason spread through matter.
No, logos only ever meant a spoken word, so the two don't connect at all.
chat.meaning: One word, different houses: for the Stoics, the divine reason pervading everything; for John, the Word who was with God and became flesh.

Heraclitus.meaning: an early Greek philosopher who saw an order running through the world

Cleanthes.meaning: an early Stoic, Zeno's successor, who wrote a hymn about the logos

Philo of Alexandria.meaning: a Jewish philosopher of John's era who wrote about the Logos

Justin.meaning: an early Christian teacher who spoke of seeds of the logos
